extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of humor theory, playwrights, wits, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Explain and apply Henri Bergson's theory of the comic: the formal mechanisms that create laughter (repetition, inversion, reciprocal interference) and their counterparts in language (wit, puns, literalizing metaphors, transposition). Useful for theorists, playwrights, and writers crafting comic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisation of life (objective of comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy aims to 'introduce mechanism into the outer forms of life' — i.e., obtain a 'mechanisation of life' by treating living behaviour as if it were mechanical, repeatable, reversible, or interchangeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use devices that make actions, relations, or persons seem rigid, automatic, or machine-like; the comic effect arises when life (normally evolving, individual, and irreversible) is represented as repeating, invertible or interchangeable. Example framing: jointed dancing-doll vs a living man. This is the overarching aim that repetition, inversion, and reciprocal interference achieve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition (comic method)
rubrics_metrics.description: A situation repeated several times in its original form, thereby contrasting with the changing stream of life; 'They are the more laughable in proportion as the scene repeated is more complex and more naturally introduced.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat a complex scene across acts or between different character-groups (e.g., masters then servants). Ensure the repetition is plausibly introduced (maintain an appearance of likelihood) yet regular enough to register as mechanical. Contemporary technique: prepare the audience's mind so coincidence becomes acceptable; classical technique: have characters' constant forces naturally cause the repetition (comedy of character).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion (comic method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reverse the situation or invert roles to produce a comic scene (e.g., prisoner lecturing magistrate; child teaching parents; robber robbed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You need not show both sides onstage; an implied or mentally reconstructed reversed scene can suffice. Often involves a character falling into his own trap (villain victim of his villainy). Inversion exploits topsyturvydom and the irony of role-reversal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal interference of series (equivocal situations)
rubrics_metrics.description: A situation is comic when it belongs simultaneously to two independent series of events and can be interpreted in two entirely different meanings at the same time — the stage-made misunderstanding is a specific case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct two independent narrative/behavioral series whose partial coincidence produces an equivocal scene. Make sure the audience can see both series (author must continually recall attention to their independence and coincidence), and create a recurring threat of breakdown that is temporarily patched, producing diversion and laughter. Use past vs present transpositions, secret subplots, or mock-heroic juxtapositions as examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absentmindedness / rigidity (source of comic)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ludicrous in events may be defined as 'absentmindedness in things' and in persons — rigidity, automatic or stereotyped action and speech are laughable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize mechanical repetition, stereotyped gestures, or 'ready-made' behavior to elicit laughter; this is the natural seed which light comedy exaggerates into art. Note: this absentmindedness is 'incurable,' so it is often only a basis for amusement rather than moral judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: comic expressed vs. comic created by language
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic EXPRESSED (can be translated) vs. comic CREATED by language (owes its being to sentence structure or word choice and is usually untranslatable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for language-specific humor, exploit idioms, grammatical gender, syntax, or phrase-forms that carry cultural or linguistic automatism; be aware such jokes may not survive translation. For more universal comic, focus on situations and actions rather than language-specific turns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witty (esprit) vs. comic (who is laughed at)
rubrics_metrics.description: A word is comic when it makes us laugh at the person who utters it, and witty when it makes us laugh at a third party or at ourselves; but often the line is blurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide target of the laugh: craft lines that either expose the speaker (comic) or pivot the joke onto someone/something else (wit). For wit, aim to compress a miniature dramatic scene into a remark that implies a wider comic situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit as dramatic miniature (method for crafting witticisms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit is 'a certain dramatic way of thinking' — a witty remark is a fugitive suggestion of a possible comic scene; to analyze a witticism, 'enlarge it into a regular scene' and identify its comic category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing a witty line, ensure it evokes an identifiable scene (robber robbed, inversion, repetition, interference). Use the technique of expanding a quip into a brief dramatic tableau to check its comic logic and force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic via absurdity fitted into ready-made phrase-forms
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic meaning is invariably obtained 'when an absurd idea is fitted into a well-established phrase-form' (i.e., an automatism is revealed by inserting an absurdity into a stock phrase).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit familiar idioms and endings; introduce an absurd or contradictory idea into a phrase the audience treats automatically (examples: 'Ce sabre est le plus beau jour de ma vie'). The comic depends on signaling the speaker's automatism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literalizing metaphors / focusing on the physical meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic effect arises 'whenever we pretend to take literally an expression which was used figuratively' — fixing attention on the physical/ material sense of a figurative phrase makes it laughable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn figurative language concrete (materialize metaphors) or choose incongruous concrete terms (gender mismatch, unfamiliar kinship term) to pull attention to the literal image. Example: treating 'all the arts are brothers' literally or twisting metaphorical verbs into concrete actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play upon words and reciprocal interference of meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: The reciprocal interference of two sets of ideas in the same sentence (pun, double meaning) generates humour: puns use homophony, while stronger play-on-words uses one sentence expressing two independent ideas due to polysemy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of degrees: the pun (two different words same sound) is a lower form; the true play-upon-words uses a single sentence with two compatible yet interfering meanings. Such devices signal a lapse of attention in language and should be used where ambiguity can be seen as negligence of language for comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion in sentence structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Inversion (putting subject in place of object and vice versa) applied to sentences produces immediate repartee or humorous refutations (e.g., 'What do you mean by emptying your pipe on to my terrace?' — 'What do you mean by putting your terrace under my pipe?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listen for reversable sentence roles and exploit them for quick retorts; this is easy, common practice among professional wits and works well for topical, responsive humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition of register/style (comic transformation of sentences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transposition is to ordinary language what repetition is to comedy: transferring ideas into a new stylistic environment or key (wrong register) while maintaining their relations makes language itself comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Move an idea into an inappropriate style or register (high style in a low context, formal phrasing for trivial content, etc.), or repeat an idea in an alien linguistic 'environment' to produce comic contrast. This is a powerful device for language-based comedy; plan the mismatch so the audience perceives both the 'natural' and the 'transposed' settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the audience perceive both series/meanings (visibility requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: For reciprocal interference, equivocality, and many witty effects to work, the audience must perceive both independent series or meanings even when the characters do not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage/publication technique: provide enough information (contextual clues, staging, wording) so the audience can hold both interpretations simultaneously; if the audience cannot see the hidden series or second meaning, the intended comic effect will fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation vs. character-driven plausibility for accepting coincidence
rubrics_metrics.description: For repeated coincidences to be accepted, either prepare the audience gradually (mesmerise the mind of the spectator) or have the characters' stable dispositions make the repetition seem natural (character forces cause repetition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using repetition, decide whether to justify the recurrence by authorial preparation (set-ups, repeated motifs) or by internal character logic; blending both produces classical resonance (comedy of character) or modern direct mind-mesmerisation (contemporary light comedy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and subtlety in wit (volatile nature of witty remarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Witty remarks are 'volatile' — they are a distilled, fleeting comic scene; try not to overexplain them: the charm lies in their rapid, delicate compression of a comic situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose witticisms that sketch the comic tableau tersely; if expanded, they reveal the underlying comic mechanism, which should be checked, but onstage/speech keep them brisk to preserve effect.
